Question 5:

[1] "Could you drink purified water made from excrement?"
 [1] ┗Yes, I can.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
 [2] Answer 5: I could drink water if it was clearly explained that the water was safe and what purposes and benefits were. For example, a video showing the purification process could be played at the place where the water is sold or used, and information about water quality, such as test results, could be provided. However if there was no explanation and the water was simply called “water made from poop”, I do not think that I would drink it. It is true that turning waste (poop) from our own bodies into water can help reduce one of the causes of pollution in rivers and oceans. However, this purification method may cost a lot of money. People like us may be reluctant to pay a high price for water, so we might hesitate to buy it, but it would be a different story if we could purify the water ourselves at a really low cost.

Summaries

five sample summaries

[1] This TED Talk is about Bill Gates’ idea to create a better toilet for people around the world. In many poor countries, people cannot afford to build sewer systems, so they have serious problems with sanitation and clean water. Bill Gates donated hundreds of millions of dollars to help develop new toilet technology. These toilets can treat human waste without needing a normal sewer system. The waste can also be used to make clean water and energy. Ronny Chieng explains this topic in a funny way, so the video does not feel too serious or difficult to understand. He also talks about microbes that can break down human waste. I was surprised that something we usually think of as useless could be turned into something useful. The video shows that toilets are not only about convenience, but also about health, water, and people’s lives.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
[2] The video introduces Bill Gates’s project to reinvent the toilet. Many poor countries can't afford to build sewer systems and it causes serious health problems. People in poor countries can’t afford to build expensive sewer systems. To solve this problem, Bill Gates thought of a project to develop toilets that don’t need a sewer system. He invested 700 million dollars in this project. Also the video shows a machine developed by scientists at the University of South Florida. Inside the machine, microbes eat human waste and it uses solar power, after turning into clear water. The microbes break down the waste and help produce clean water. In this process, we can get not only clear water, but also nutrition and energy. Also the video shows Bill Gates drinking the purified water produced from human waste. The video shows that modern technology can make it possible to reuse waste and help solve health problems around the world.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
[3] Bill Gates wants to reinvent the toilet because billions of people around the world do not have access to proper toilets. In poor countries, many communities cannot afford to build sewer systems, which can lead to the spread of diseases. To solve this problem, Gates started the Reinvent the Toilet Challenge and provided several hundred million dollars to support scientists who are developing toilets that do not need sewers. At the University of South Florida, Professor Daniel Yeh and his team are developing a machine that treats human waste. Microorganisms inside a bioreactor break down the waste and turn it into clean water. The system can use solar power, and the process can also produce nutrients and methane. Methane can be burned to create energy. The team is even working with NASA to explore how this technology can be used in space. During the interview, comedian Ronny Chieng jokes about the project and suggests funny ideas, such as planes powered by human waste. However, Gates explains that the technology must be affordable so that the poorest communities can use it. He also describes projects that are being tested in Durban, South Africa, where some residents lack proper sewage treatment. At the end of the interview, Chieng drinks water that has been processed by the machine. He says that it tastes like ordinary water. The video shows that reinventing toilets is not just about convenience. It can also help improve sanitation, prevent diseases, and turn human waste into useful resources.
[4] Bill Gates talks about the importance of reinventing the toilet.Before,while giving a speech,he put his poop on the platform. Many people in developing countries find it difficult to connect public health. They struggle with diseases. However, the system of new toilets Bill thought is not so expensive and can produce energy and clean water,so we can solve health issues gradually if the new toilets can be accepted. The water is so clean that people can drink it. New ideas using poop were introduced.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       
[5] In this video, the interviewer talks with the speaker about a project to reinvent the toilet for poor countries. Millions of people around the world still lack proper sanitation because building traditional sewer systems are far too expensive. To solve this problem, the speaker has invested hundreds of millions of dollars into developing new technology that processes human waste without needing water or sewers. The interviewer visits a university laboratory to see special bioreactor that uses microorganisms to break down human feces. Surprisingly, this machine turns waste into clean drinking water and natural gas, which can be used as energy. Although the interviewer makes lighthearted jokes throughout the discussion, the speaker explains that keeping the technology cheap is essential so that the poorest communities can benefit from it. In the end, the interviewer drinks purified water created by the machine and agrees that this innovation could change the future for millions of people.

Opinions

five sample opinions

[1]                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     
[2] I think this is very interesting because it can help people who do not have safe toilets. Before watching this video, I did not know that human waste could be turned into clean water and energy. At first, I felt uncomfortable about drinking water made from poop. However, I think it is a good idea if the water is completely purified and safe. I also learned that people in poor countries face serious sanitation problems.I believe governments and scientists should work together to develop affordable technology. This project could improve people’s health and protect the environment.                                                                                                           
[3] I am for the installation of the reinvented toilets. In modern times, the need for sustainable energy is growing as the situation of global warming is getting worse. There are a variety of types of sustainable energy such as solar, water, and wind power. However, each of these has cons; solar power and wind power are subject to fluctuation depending on the weather and hydropower needs large land for the dumps. On the other hand, reinvested toilets do not need that much land, nor is it affected by the weather, which means it can be installed everywhere in the world. Therefore reinvented toilets are a good solution not only for sanitation in poor communities and the global environment.
[4] I think the process is needed in developed countries too. This is because the environment is not good in poor countries. Furthermore, they can get diseases easily and I suggest their health is not good. That is why I think the project is great for poor people. If the clean water was poop, it is good for poor people instead of river’ s water that is not maintained. I think the toilets should be used in riverbeds. I used to go to riverbeds to play sports. There were toilets, but the toilets were terrible, because the air’ s smell was uncomfortable. That is why the Japanese or zone government should conduct these. The change of sanitary space leads to long life.                         
[5] I am impressed by how this project transforms environmental hazards into valuable resources. In the video, advanced toilets use microorganisms to convert human waste into clean water, natural gas, and natural resources without requiring massive sewage infrastructure.Testing this technology in Durban, South Africa demonstrates its real-world potential to protect local ecosystems from water pollution and reduce disease. By turning dangerous waste into renewable energy and safe water, this system promotes a circular economy. I believe such off-grid innovations are essential for fighting climate change and achieving sustainable resource management in developing regions and beyond.
